Transformer pruning pipelines typically remove attention heads iteratively — score each head by some importance criterion (gradient magnitude, Taylor expansion, activation variance), excise the lowest-scoring fraction, fine-tune to recover, then repeat. The central question is whether successive pruning rounds are making independent, locally-correct decisions or whether they are compounding errors: heads that looked redundant in round k only appeared redundant because other heads were already removed in round k−1, artificially inflating those survivors' apparent importance and masking true redundancy elsewhere. The key concepts are head importance non-stationarity (a head's measured contribution shifts as the surrounding population changes), importance score coupling (heads that attend to overlapping query-key subspaces will show correlated importance fluctuations across rounds), and functional redundancy amplification (iterative removal concentrates the remaining heads into fewer distinct functional roles, paradoxically making the network appear less redundant than a fresh single-pass evaluation would suggest). What a beginner misses is that importance scores are not properties of individual heads — they are relational quantities defined over the current head population, so reusing the same scoring metric across iterations without reweighting for population shift produces systematic bias toward under-pruning early functional clusters and over-pruning late-round survivors. The expert worries specifically about irreversible capacity collapse: once the network's residual stream is dominated by a narrow cluster of high-overlap heads, fine-tuning can recover loss metrics while silently destroying representational diversity, leaving a model that benchmarks acceptably but fails catastrophically under distribution shift.

This coupling is not symmetric: the head with slightly lower baseline importance gets removed first, which transfers functional load to its near-duplicate neighbor, artificially elevating that neighbor's score and shielding it from subsequent pruning rounds even if it carries genuinely redundant information relative to the remaining population. Michel et al. The propagation compounds geometrically: if a layer begins with three near-duplicate heads and you remove one per round, each removal tightens the coupling between the survivors, so by round three you are making a pruning decision on a head whose importance score reflects the cumulative load-transfer of two prior removals, not its intrinsic contribution. This implies a concrete removal-order pathology: iterative pruners systematically defer removing the last member of a functional cluster because that member's score is inflated by absorbed load, while aggressively removing heads from underrepresented functional roles that show lower scores precisely because they are doing something nobody else is doing. The practical consequence, visible in structured pruning benchmarks on BERT-base and RoBERTa (see Voita et al. 2019 on syntactic head specialization), is that compressed models disproportionately retain syntactic-pattern heads (which cluster and cross-elevate each other) while losing positional and rare-token heads that were functionally unique and uncoupled.

Fine-tuning after each pruning round operates under two constraints that prevent genuine functional redistribution: parameter locality (the surviving head's W_Q, W_K, W_V matrices are the only parameters that can absorb the lost head's function, since the pruned head's parameters are gone) and loss surface flatness in the absorbed-load direction (once a survivor has expanded its effective receptive field to cover the pruned head's patterns, the gradient signal for redistributing that function elsewhere is near-zero because the loss is already satisfied). The key mechanism is what Guo et al. (2019, "Retraining-based Iterative Pruning") implicitly demonstrate: short fine-tuning schedules — typically 1–3% of original training compute per round, the industry norm — are insufficient to escape the local basin the survivor landed in after absorbing load, because the learning rate is decayed and the optimizer state (Adam's second moment estimate) has adapted to the post-absorption gradient landscape, making large directional moves costly. Even with longer fine-tuning, residual stream bottlenecking intervenes: if layer l has lost heads that were projecting into specific subspaces of the residual stream, the downstream layers have already begun compensating via their own weight updates, creating a cross-layer co-adaptation that makes unilateral redistribution within layer l destabilizing — a phenomenon related to the "layer co-adaptation" problem documented in lottery ticket literature (Frankle & Carlin, 2019). The coupling bias therefore does not reset between rounds; it stratifies: each fine-tuning phase locks in the load-transfer state as a new local minimum, and the importance scorer in the next round treats that locked state as ground truth, inheriting all accumulated bias. Empirically, this shows up as the well-known "pruning cliff" — models that compress gracefully to 50% head count and then degrade sharply — because by that point every surviving head is a load-bearing last-cluster-member whose importance score reflects three or four rounds of accumulated inflation with no redistribution, and removing any one of them triggers cascading loss spikes that short fine-tuning cannot recover.

Optimizer reinitialization does partially break stratification — resetting Adam's second moment estimate removes the artificially low effective learning rate in directions the optimizer had deemed "settled," allowing the fine-tuning phase to make larger moves in subspaces that were previously locked — but the relief is incomplete because the weight values themselves encode the absorbed-load state, and a fresh optimizer exploring from that weight initialization will rediscover approximately the same basin unless the learning rate is high enough to escape it, which conflicts with the stability requirements of a partially-pruned network. Raghu et al.'s work on loss landscape geometry and the more directly relevant findings from "Revisiting the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis" (Frankle et al., 2020) suggest that late-stage networks have sharp, narrow loss basins where even aggressive reinitialization with high LR causes loss spikes that exceed what short recovery budgets can absorb — meaning the practical escape radius from optimizer reset is smaller than the distance to a genuinely redistributed functional state. The reason standard pipelines avoid optimizer reinitialization is threefold and concrete: first, it increases per-round compute significantly because a cold optimizer requires more steps to converge, violating the 1–3% compute budget norm; second, practitioners observe that reinitialized fine-tuning produces higher loss variance across random seeds, making pipeline outcomes harder to reproduce and certify for production deployment; third, most pruning pipelines are benchmarked on final task metrics alone, so the hidden cost of stratification accumulation is invisible until the pruning cliff, at which point the diagnosis is attributed to "over-pruning" rather than coupling bias. There is a middle path — partial optimizer reset, where second moments are reset but first moments (momentum) are retained — that some recent work (e.g., SparseGPT-adjacent methods from Frantar & Alistarh, 2023) implicitly gestures toward, but it remains non-standard because the interaction between retained momentum and fresh curvature estimates is poorly characterized theoretically. The deeper reason standard pipelines don't address this is that the field has optimized for single-metric leaderboard performance on fixed benchmarks, where a model that has silently lost representational diversity but retained accuracy on in-distribution eval looks identical to one that has not — the stratification cost only manifests under distribution shift or downstream fine-tuning, which most compression benchmarks never measure.

A pruning-aware perturbation scheme needs to satisfy three simultaneous constraints: it must move weights in directions orthogonal to the current task loss gradient (to avoid immediate loss spikes), aligned with the subspaces vacated by pruned heads (to redistribute absorbed function rather than just adding noise), and scaled to the local loss curvature (so perturbation magnitude stays within the flat region of the basin before the recovery optimizer takes over). The closest existing framework is the second-order weight perturbation used in Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS, Hassibi & Stork 1993) and its modern revival in SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2022), where the inverse Hessian H⁻¹ is used to compute a closed-form weight update that compensates for a removed parameter with zero first-order loss change — but OBS/SparseGPT apply this at the moment of pruning to compensate for the removed head's direct output, not to perturb survivors away from their absorbed-load basin, which is a fundamentally different target. What is needed is an asymmetric perturbation: immediately after pruning head i, compute the null space of the surviving heads' collective output projection onto the residual stream, then inject a small perturbation into each survivor's W_V matrix along directions in that null space weighted by how much of head i's pre-pruning output variance lived there — this moves survivors toward covering vacated representational territory without changing their current residual stream contribution, keeping loss flat while opening the basin. The loss-spike risk is controlled by perturbation magnitude scheduling: the Hessian diagonal (cheap to approximate via Fisher information on a small calibration set, as in GPTQ) tells you the curvature in the perturbation direction, and you scale perturbation to stay within the region where quadratic approximation holds — empirically this means perturbations on the order of 1–5% of the weight norm in low-curvature directions are safe, a threshold that standard random noise perturbations routinely violate. No deployed pipeline implements this fully, but the pieces exist: GPTQ provides the curvature estimates, the SVD of pruned head outputs provides the target subspace, and the null-space projection is straightforward — the gap is that these components have never been composed into a single inter-round perturbation step because the field conceptualizes pruning and fine-tuning as strictly sequential phases rather than as a coupled weight-trajectory problem. The practical obstacle is calibration data dependency: computing the Fisher approximation and the pruned head's output SVD requires a representative data sample at each round, adding pipeline complexity and raising the question of whether the calibration distribution itself introduces bias into which subspaces are deemed vacated — a subtle but real failure mode if the calibration set underrepresents domain-specific attention patterns the pruned head was handling.

The vacated-subspace estimate is computed via SVD of the pruned head's output activations on the calibration set, and its sensitivity follows a well-characterized statistical threshold: the top singular vectors stabilize quickly (requiring roughly 2–4× the head's output dimension in samples, so ~256–512 samples for a 64-dim head in BERT-base), but the tail singular vectors — which represent rare, low-variance attention patterns — require sample counts that scale with the inverse of their singular value gap, meaning a calibration set of 128–256 samples (the GPTQ default) will reliably miss subspace directions corresponding to infrequent but functionally critical patterns like rare-token attention or long-range syntactic dependencies. Distribution mismatch compounds this differently than size: a calibration set drawn from a single domain will estimate a subspace that reflects that domain's attention statistics, so the "vacated" directions identified are those unused in that domain, and perturbations targeting them will push survivors toward covering domain-specific patterns the pruned head handled elsewhere — effectively encoding the calibration distribution's blind spots into the weight trajectory as a permanent bias. This does compound across rounds, but with a distinct structure from importance score bias: importance score coupling compounds multiplicatively (each round's scores are conditioned on all prior removals), whereas subspace estimation error compounds additively with drift — each round's perturbation is off by some angular error ε_k relative to the true vacated subspace, and those angular errors accumulate in the residual stream's representational geometry, progressively rotating the surviving heads' effective coverage away from the true functional partition of the original model. Rasley et al.'s ZeroQuant and related calibration-sensitive compression work suggest that beyond ~4 rounds of iterative perturbation with fixed calibration data, the accumulated subspace drift becomes detectable as increased perplexity variance on held-out domains even when in-distribution metrics are flat — a signal that the residual stream geometry has been systematically skewed rather than uniformly compressed. The critical asymmetry that makes this worse than importance score bias is non-recoverability: a miscalibrated importance score in round k merely causes a suboptimal pruning choice that fine-tuning partially corrects, but a miscalibrated subspace perturbation in round k physically moves weights in the wrong direction and those moves are then treated as the new baseline for round k+1's curvature estimates, meaning subsequent rounds are optimizing against a corrupted loss landscape model rather than just a corrupted selection criterion.

A principled detection criterion exists and can be constructed from two measurable quantities: the Hessian trace ratio between successive rounds (TrH_k / TrH_{k-1}, approximated cheaply via Hutchinson's estimator on the surviving parameters) and the inter-round weight displacement angle (the cosine distance between the fine-tuning trajectory direction in round k and round k-1). When the Hessian trace ratio exceeds ~1.3–1.5 — meaning the loss landscape has become sharper rather than flatter after a round of pruning and recovery — this signals that the fine-tuning is no longer finding a genuine local minimum but is instead oscillating near a saddle region created by subspace corruption; simultaneously, if the fine-tuning trajectory angle flips by more than ~40–60 degrees between rounds, the optimizer is compensating for geometric drift rather than recovering task performance. This combination is more reliable than monitoring validation loss alone because validation loss can remain flat while both signals spike, exactly the regime where the residual stream geometry is corrupting silently — analogous to how Izmailov et al.'s stochastic weight averaging work showed that loss-flat regions can have dramatically different geometric properties that only manifest under perturbation or distribution shift. When these thresholds are crossed, halting iterative pruning and switching strategy is empirically justified, and the concrete alternative is one-shot structured pruning with global importance ranking (score all heads jointly on the current corrupted-but-stable model, remove the target fraction simultaneously, run a single longer fine-tuning), which sidesteps compounding by treating accumulated drift as a fixed starting point rather than an ongoing process — this is effectively what makes SparseGPT's single-pass approach outperform iterative magnitude pruning at high sparsity ratios on LLaMA-scale models. The detection criterion should trigger a strategy switch rather than a halt in most practical settings, because halting leaves the model at an intermediate compression ratio that may satisfy neither the deployment compute budget nor the accuracy requirement — the corrupted landscape is a better initialization for one-shot pruning than random initialization, so the accumulated rounds are not wasted even when further iteration is counterproductive. What the field lacks is a standardized drift audit protocol: currently no major pruning library (neither HuggingFace's optimum, nor Neural Magic's SparseML, nor MIT HAN Lab's tools) computes inter-round Hessian trace ratios or trajectory angles as monitoring outputs, so practitioners have no dashboard signal for when the iterative regime has become self-defeating — the detection criterion is theoretically available but operationally invisible.

Global joint scoring does not neutralize the subspace bias — it merely changes its expression. In iterative pruning, coupling bias manifests as temporal inflation (survivors' scores rise across rounds due to load transfer); in one-shot scoring on the corrupted model, the same coupling manifests as spatial inflation (heads that absorbed load in prior iterative rounds have higher activation variance and output norms baked into their weights, so they score higher in a joint ranking even though their elevated scores reflect accumulated transfer rather than intrinsic importance). The one-shot ranker sees a population of heads where the iterative rounds have already destroyed the score independence that joint ranking assumes — specifically, the corrupted model's weight geometry means that heads from over-represented functional clusters (which survived iterative rounds by mutual importance inflation) present artificially high joint scores, while the few remaining heads from under-represented functional roles present depressed scores because their weights were perturbed toward covering vacated subspaces rather than deepening their native function. Michel et al.'s sensitivity analysis framework and the Taylor expansion scoring used in, e.g., Molchanov et al. (2019) both assume that importance scores reflect the current model's functional partition — but on a corruption-initialized model, the functional partition itself has been distorted, so a globally computed Taylor score is measuring importance within a corrupted geometry, not within the geometry of a model that was trained end-to-end at the target compression ratio. The concrete consequence is that one-shot pruning on the corrupted initialization will systematically over-retain the same heads that the iterative phase protected — the last survivors of high-overlap functional clusters — because their weight-encoded load absorption gives them high output sensitivity regardless of scoring method, producing a compressed model with the same representational narrowness that the strategy switch was meant to escape. The only intervention that genuinely breaks this inheritance is re-anchoring the importance scores to a reference model — specifically, computing score differentials between the corrupted model and a lightweight proxy of the original pre-pruning model (or an EMA checkpoint from early in the iterative phase), so that heads whose scores are elevated purely due to accumulated load transfer are identified and discounted; this is conceptually related to the "relative importance" framing in some continual learning literature but has not been formalized for pruning pipelines.
